tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

schema.name: Workflow
schema.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

The Old Bull course is reviewed and written up, and none of your follow-up actions have been started yet. All of it was done in one session yesterday (9/24). It lives in `DEV/RunningTheRoom`, which is up to date with GitHub.

## What the course is
"Running The Room" is Dr Jason Weber's Old Bull Performance course on leading a high-performance department. It has 31 lessons and 26 PDFs across four modules. The videos and PDFs stay on Drive at `09_PRO_DEV\Old bull performance`. The repo holds only the analysis, because it's a paid course.

## What's done
1. **Module notes.** Fable 5.1 read every lesson and PDF and wrote notes for each module in `notes/module-1..4.md`. It also wrote a brief on your situation in `notes/eric-context.md`.
2. **Three documents in `docs/`:**
   - `00_what_this_is.md`: a short summary of the course and the tools worth keeping.
   - `01_department_plan.md`: a four-phase plan for your department:
     - common language and people
     - measurement discipline
     - a regular meeting rhythm
     - how decisions get made and who makes them

### 3. Knowledge-Behaviour Matrix (Webinar Parts II and III, Lab 1B, Student Workbook)

What it is: a grid for auditing yourself and your staff on two independent axes. It evaluates capability and engagement, not personal worth.

Knowledge axis (categories PDF-confirmed; the horizontal-axis placement comes from the webinar transcript only):

- **Knowledge:** Handbrake, Pawn, Practitioner, Operator. An Operator can design, integrate and troubleshoot complex systems and sees how technology, training and operations connect.
- **Behaviour:** Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst. A Catalyst creates movement, influences others, and finds the path forward.

## B1. Where I sit now

**Knowledge: Practitioner.**
I understand our tools, our context and our environment. I can help solve problems, build frameworks, and have useful conversations about them. Where I stall is the last step of execution. I have many ideas and many ways to integrate things at a conceptual and theoretical level, but getting them over the final hump into something that bears fruit is where I fall short. By the course's own test, I am not yet an Operator: the systems I build would not keep running without me.

I work to create movement and influence others: I mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas to leadership, put together solution proposals, learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of that back here, and bring new ideas and organisational structures into the conversation. ## B2. Evidence

**Knowledge (what I actually do):**
- Built the football GPS and force-plate data pipelines myself.
- Built the PFF database and the EPA matchup profiles used in weekly game preparation.
- Designed the volleyball monitoring framework with Coach Mike Wenger so that he runs it end to end: he collects, cleans, exports and imports the data. My part is routine maintenance and one spreadsheet button he could press himself. This is the one system I have built that would keep running without me, which is the Operator test.

**Behaviour (how I show up):**
- Mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas and solution proposals to leadership.
- Learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of it back here.
- **What stuck:** the volleyball framework. It was built with its daily user, and he owns it.
- **What faded:** the technology framework and much of the reporting we discussed; the DEXA project on using body composition to profile athlete potential; a website; a newsletter; an auditing framework for departmental objectives. Each was pushed early and went nowhere.

**Why the difference.** The one that stuck had a co-owner from the start who used it every day and needed it. The ones that faded were mine alone: no one else to support them, carry them or ask for them. I have been trying to get things off the ground by myself, without much success. I need a co-pilot, a co-champion attached to each project who has real weight behind it.

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Started 2026-09-25. Professional development folder item, due 2026-09-30.

Source: Old Bull Performance, *Running The Room*, Module 1, Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook (sections B1 to B3 and D1). Private. Section C (rating other people) is deliberately not done.

## The two axes

- **Knowledge:** Handbrake, Pawn, Practitioner, Operator. An Operator can design, integrate and troubleshoot complex systems and sees how technology, training and operations connect.
- **Behaviour:** Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst. A Catalyst creates movement, influences others, and finds the path forward.

## B1. Where I sit now

**Knowledge: Practitioner.**
I understand our tools, our context and our environment. I can help solve problems, build frameworks, and have useful conversations about them. Where I stall is the last step of execution. I have many ideas and many ways to integrate things at a conceptual and theoretical level, but getting them over the final hump into something that bears fruit is where I fall short. By the course's own test, I am not yet an Operator: the systems I build would not keep running without me.

**Behaviour: Catalyst in effort, not yet in outcome.**
I work to create movement and influence others: I mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas to leadership, put together solution proposals, learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of that back here, and bring new ideas and organisational structures into the conversation. But when I ask whether the change sticks, the honest answer is often no. The workbook offers only three levels and I am clearly not a Coaster, so Catalyst is the placement, with the caveat that my evidence is mostly inputs (proposals, presentations, conversations) rather than changes that lasted.

**The common thread.** Both axes point at the same gap: turning ideas into things that run and last without me. That gap separates Practitioner from Operator, and it is also what separates pushing for change from change that sticks.

# Knowledge-Behaviour Self-Audit

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Started 2026-09-25. Professional development folder item, due 2026-09-30.

Source: Old Bull Performance, *Running The Room*, Module 1, Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook (sections B1 to B3 and D1). Private. Section C (rating other people) is deliberately not done.

## The two axes

- **Knowledge:** Handbrake, Pawn, Practitioner, Operator. An Operator can design, integrate and troubleshoot complex systems and sees how technology, training and operations connect.
- **Behaviour:** Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst. A Catalyst creates movement, influences others, and finds the path forward.

## B1. Where I sit now

**Knowledge: Practitioner.**
I understand our tools, our context and our environment. I can help solve problems, build frameworks, and have useful conversations about them. Where I stall is the last step of execution. I have many ideas and many ways to integrate things at a conceptual and theoretical level, but getting them over the final hump into something that bears fruit is where I fall short. By the course's own test, I am not yet an Operator: the systems I build would not keep running without me.

**Behaviour: Catalyst in effort, not yet in outcome.**
I work to create movement and influence others: I mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas to leadership, put together solution proposals, learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of that back here, and bring new ideas and organisational structures into the conversation. But when I ask whether the change sticks, the honest answer is often no. The workbook offers only three levels and I am clearly not a Coaster, so Catalyst is the placement, with the caveat that my evidence is mostly inputs (proposals, presentations, conversations) rather than changes that lasted.

**The common thread.** Both axes point at the same gap: turning ideas into things that run and last without me. That gap separates Practitioner from Operator, and it is also what separates pushing for change from change that sticks.

## B2. Evidence

**Knowledge (what I actually do):**
- Built the football GPS and force-plate data pipelines myself.
- Built the PFF database and the EPA matchup profiles used in weekly game preparation.
- Designed the volleyball monitoring framework with Coach Mike Wenger so that he runs it end to end: he collects, cleans, exports and imports the data. My part is routine maintenance and one spreadsheet button he could press himself. This is the one system I have built that would keep running without me, which is the Operator test.

**Behaviour (how I show up):**
- Mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas and solution proposals to leadership.
- Learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of it back here.
- **What stuck:** the volleyball framework. It was built with its daily user, and he owns it.
- **What faded:** the technology framework and much of the reporting we discussed; the DEXA project on using body composition to profile athlete potential; a website; a newsletter; an auditing framework for departmental objectives. Each was pushed early and went nowhere.

**Why the difference.** The one that stuck had a co-owner from the start who used it every day and needed it. The ones that faded were mine alone: no one else to support them, carry them or ask for them. I have been trying to get things off the ground by myself, without much success. I need a co-pilot, a co-champion attached to each project who has real weight behind it.

# Knowledge-Behaviour Self-Audit

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Started 2026-09-25. Professional development folder item, due 2026-09-30.

Source: Old Bull Performance, *Running The Room*, Module 1, Knowledge_Behaviour_Profile_Student_Workbook (sections B1 to B3 and D1). Private. Section C (rating other people) is deliberately not done.

## The two axes

- **Knowledge:** Handbrake, Pawn, Practitioner, Operator. An Operator can design, integrate and troubleshoot complex systems and sees how technology, training and operations connect.
- **Behaviour:** Misaligned, Coaster, Catalyst. A Catalyst creates movement, influences others, and finds the path forward.

## B1. Where I sit now

**Knowledge: Practitioner.**
I understand our tools, our context and our environment. I can help solve problems, build frameworks, and have useful conversations about them. Where I stall is the last step of execution. I have many ideas and many ways to integrate things at a conceptual and theoretical level, but getting them over the final hump into something that bears fruit is where I fall short. By the course's own test, I am not yet an Operator: the systems I build would not keep running without me.

**Behaviour: Catalyst in effort, not yet in outcome.**
I work to create movement and influence others: I mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas to leadership, put together solution proposals, learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of that back here, and bring new ideas and organisational structures into the conversation. But when I ask whether the change sticks, the honest answer is often no. The workbook offers only three levels and I am clearly not a Coaster, so Catalyst is the placement, with the caveat that my evidence is mostly inputs (proposals, presentations, conversations) rather than changes that lasted.

**The common thread.** Both axes point at the same gap: turning ideas into things that run and last without me. That gap separates Practitioner from Operator, and it is also what separates pushing for change from change that sticks.

## B2. Evidence

**Knowledge (what I actually do):**
- Built the football GPS and force-plate data pipelines myself.
- Built the PFF database and the EPA matchup profiles used in weekly game preparation.
- Designed the volleyball monitoring framework with Coach Mike Wenger so that he runs it end to end: he collects, cleans, exports and imports the data. My part is routine maintenance and one spreadsheet button he could press himself. This is the one system I have built that would keep running without me, which is the Operator test.

**Behaviour (how I show up):**
- Mentor younger staff, speak up in meetings, present ideas and solution proposals to leadership.
- Learn from people much further along in their careers and bring pieces of it back here.
- **What stuck:** the volleyball framework. It was built with its daily user, and he owns it.
- **What faded:** the technology framework and much of the reporting we discussed; the DEXA project on using body composition to profile athlete potential; a website; a newsletter; an auditing framework for departmental objectives. Each was pushed early and went nowhere.

**Why the difference.** The one that stuck had a co-owner from the start who used it every day and needed it. The ones that faded were mine alone: no one else to support them, carry them or ask for them. I have been trying to get things off the ground by myself, without much success. I need a co-pilot, a co-champion attached to each project who has real weight behind it.

## B3. Where I want to be in 3 to 5 years

**Knowledge: Operator. Behaviour: Catalyst, in outcome and not only in effort.**

**What would need to change:** I need to start shipping. I have a whiteboard full of ideas, projects and tasks. I need to see them through to completion in an ordered way, push them out, and expose people to them, instead of keeping a half-finished list that nobody else knows about, which is where I am now. The principle is "Always Be Shipping," from Seth Godin's idea of shipping: finish the idea, put it in front of people, move on to the next one. Some of what I ship will stick, or grow from other people's input, and turn from a one-off project into something sustainable. At the least it creates value, and the visible sense of value, so that others here and at other institutions pick up on it and I can help where I am needed.

**The check from B2:** shipping alone to no one is how the five faded projects died. So each thing I ship goes to a named person who will use it, the way the volleyball framework went to Coach Wenger. Ship to someone, not into the air.

## D1. Three actions in the next 30 to 90 days

*Pending.*

Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.

- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.

Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".

Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">

**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
```
